section_1.title: The Intuition: Contextual Focus
section_1.content: Introduce the problem: Traditional models process words in isolation. Use the concept of 'selective focus' to explain how we read human language by prioritizing relevant words.
section_1.example: In the sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', a human instantly knows 'it' refers to the 'animal'. We show a visual spotlight moving from 'it' to 'animal'.

section_2.title: The Query, Key, and Value Metaphor
section_2.content: Explain the mechanics using a library/database search analogy. Define Query (what I'm looking for), Key (the tag on the book), and Value (the content inside).
section_2.example: Imagine a library: Your 'Query' is the search bar term, the 'Key' is the book spine label, and the 'Value' is the actual information written on the pages.

section_3.title: Visualizing the Calculation: Scaled Dot-Product
section_3.content: Briefly introduce the math as a vector alignment exercise. Explain that high similarity (dot product) = high attention weight. Show the formula: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √dₖ)V as a weighted sum.
section_3.example: Represent Q and K as arrows in a 2D plane. Use a 'cosine similarity' visual where the angle between arrows determines the 'brightness' of the attention weight.

section_4.title: Softmax and Weight Normalization
section_4.content: Explain why we use Softmax: to ensure all attention weights sum up to 100% (probability distribution).
section_4.example: Use a bar chart animation where 'it' distributes focus across the whole sentence, with the tallest bar highlighting 'animal' (0.8) and smaller bars for 'street' (0.1) and 'tired' (0.1).

section_5.title: Synthesis: From One Word to Understanding
section_5.content: Conclude by showing how Multi-Head Attention allows the model to look at different parts of the sentence simultaneously (e.g., one head focuses on grammar, another on semantic meaning).
section_5.example: A visual split-screen showing a robot reading the same sentence: Head 1 links pronouns, Head 2 links causal relationships, resulting in a deeper, multi-dimensional representation of the sentence.
